c.tagline: Britain's harbourside capital of street art, music, and maker culture.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed Hackney cabs are metered and can be hailed or found at ranks; private-hire cars must be pre-booked. Uber and Bolt operate citywide.

emergency.note: Dial 999 for police, fire, or ambulance; use NHS 111 for urgent but non-life-threatening medical advice.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The Harbourside and Park Street bar areas get rowdy late, and Stokes Croft/St Pauls warrant awareness after dark.

hood_desc: The revitalised waterfront at the heart of the city, ringed by the M Shed and We The Curious museums, the SS Great Britain, and quayside bars and restaurants; the central, walkable base for a first visit.
The genteel Georgian hilltop village above the Avon Gorge, famous for the Clifton Suspension Bridge, crescents of pale stone, antique shops, and the zoo; scenic and refined.
The raw, creative artery north of the centre, plastered with murals (including Banksy's), lined with independent cafes, record shops, and some of the city's edgiest nightlife.
The medieval commercial core around cobbled King Street, home to the Old Vic theatre, centuries-old pubs, and the covered St Nicholas Market; lively and full of history.
The up-and-coming, family-friendly quarters south of the harbour, centred on North Street's independent shops, the Tobacco Factory, and street-art murals; laid-back and local.
lodging: Mercure Bristol Holland House Hotel & Spa

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the UK.

transit.hours: Buses run from around 5:00am to about 11:30pm on core routes, with limited night services at weekends; the harbour ferry runs mainly in daylight hours.
transit.note: Bristol Ferry Boats hop between harbourside piers (Temple Meads, city centre, SS Great Britain, Hotwells) — as much a scenic ride as everyday transport.
transit.pay: Bristol has no metro or tram; First Bus runs most services — tap a contactless card or pay the driver, with a daily fare cap, or buy an mTicket (a day ticket is about £5) in the First Bus app. MetroBus rapid routes use off-bus ticket machines. Local trains from Temple Meads serve the wider area.

transit.m: Bristol Airport Flyer (A1) bus to Temple Meads & city centre (~30 min, every 10-20 min)

tip.r: ~10-12.5% at restaurants if a service charge isn't already added; no need to tip when ordering at the bar in a pub.

food.name: Pie and mash
food.desc: Bristol's own pie culture: steak and ale or chicken and cider pies with mash, mushy peas and gravy. Pieminister was founded here in 2003.

places.name: Pieminister
places.note: The original market stall of the Bristol-born pie company; award-winning pies with mash, peas and gravy.

places.name: Pieminister Stokes Croft
places.note: Sit-down cafe version of the same pies with a bar and a livelier local crowd.

places.name: Buxton and Bird
places.note: Butcher-led pies eaten in or taken away; pie, mash, gravy and a beer for around ten pounds.

food.name: Jamaican patties and jerk chicken
food.desc: Bristol's Caribbean community, centred on St Pauls, gave the city flaky curried-beef patties, jerk chicken, curry goat and rice and peas.

places.name: Caribbean Croft
places.note: Long-running Caribbean kitchen and rum bar; jerk chicken, curry goat and patties, with live music.

places.name: Rice and Things
places.note: Home-style Jamaican cooking that locals rate highly; small room, so book or take away.

places.name: St Pauls Carnival street stalls
places.note: Early July only, but the best day of the year for patties, jerk pans and rum punch.

food.name: Sunday roast
food.desc: Bristol takes its roast seriously: West Country beef or pork, roast potatoes in dripping, a Yorkshire pudding the size of a hat and cauliflower cheese.

places.name: The Bank Tavern
places.note: Tiny pub whose roast became famous nationwide; book far ahead or try midweek.

places.name: The Kensington Arms
places.note: Smart neighbourhood pub with a consistently excellent roast and proper gravy.

places.name: The Cottage Inn
places.note: Waterside pub reachable by ferry; roasts with a view across the floating harbour.

food.name: West Country cheddar and a ploughman's
food.desc: Somerset cheddar aged in Cheddar Gorge caves, plus Bath soft cheese and Gorwydd Caerphilly, eaten with pickle, bread and a pint of cider.

places.name: The Bristol Cheesemonger
places.note: Excellent counter of West Country farmhouse cheeses; will build a board to eat in.

places.name: St Nicholas Market
places.note: Cheese and deli stalls in the Georgian market halls; good for assembling a picnic.

places.name: Source Food Hall
places.note: Butcher, cheese counter and cafe under one roof, strong on regional producers.

food.name: Fish and chips and harbourside seafood
food.desc: Cornish-landed cod and haddock in beer batter, plus mussels, crab and oysters from the South West coast eaten beside the floating harbour.

places.name: The Salt and Malt
places.note: Harbourside chippy and seafood bar doing proper batter and West Country shellfish.

places.name: Cargo, Wapping Wharf
places.note: Shipping-container food strip on the water with several seafood and small-plate kitchens.

places.name: St Nicholas Market
places.note: Lunchtime stalls including fish counters; cheapest sit-down-free way to eat well in the centre.

food.name: West Country cream tea
food.desc: Warm scones with clotted cream and strawberry jam, taken with a pot of tea. In the West Country the cream goes on first, whatever Cornwall says.

places.name: Primrose Cafe
places.note: Long-established village cafe with terrace tables; classic scones and cakes.

places.name: Boston Tea Party
places.note: Bristol-founded cafe group; reliable scones and coffee in a Georgian townhouse.

places.name: Cox and Baloney
places.note: Vintage tearoom doing full afternoon-tea stands as well as single scones.

food.name: West Country cider
food.desc: Bristol is the gateway to Somerset's orchards: still farmhouse scrumpy, sharp Kingston Black and modern keeved ciders, poured by the pint everywhere.

places.name: The Apple
places.note: Cider bar on a moored barge with dozens of West Country ciders; a Bristol rite of passage.

places.name: The Orchard Inn
places.note: Backstreet cider specialist with a huge rotating range and good-value bar snacks.

places.name: Bristol Cider Shop
places.note: Bottle shop and tasting room focused on small West Country producers; staff know their orchards.

food.name: Bristol Cream sherry
food.desc: Sherry was landed, blended and bottled in Bristol's docks for centuries, giving the world Bristol Milk and Harveys Bristol Cream.

places.name: Bravas
places.note: Spanish tapas bar with a serious sherry list poured by the copita; the best place to explore the style.

places.name: Averys of Bristol
places.note: Wine merchant trading in Bristol since 1793, still selling sherry and port to the city.

places.name: Hyde and Co
places.note: Hidden cocktail bar that treats sherry and fortified wines seriously in its drinks.

landmarks: Clifton Suspension Bridge
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's iconic Victorian suspension bridge spans the dramatic Avon Gorge and is the defining symbol of Bristol.
SS Great Britain
Brunel's revolutionary 19th-century iron-hulled steamship, now beautifully restored and on display in the very dry dock where it was built.
Bristol Cathedral
A striking medieval cathedral on College Green renowned for its unique hall-church design and centuries of history.
St Mary Redcliffe Church
Once called 'the fairest, goodliest parish church in England' by Elizabeth I, this Gothic masterpiece dominates Bristol's skyline.
Clifton Observatory & Camera Obscura
A historic windmill-turned-observatory perched above the Avon Gorge, offering a Victorian camera obscura and sweeping views of the suspension bridge.
Cabot Tower, Brandon Hill
A Victorian sandstone tower atop the city's oldest park, rewarding climbers with 360-degree views across Bristol's rooftops and harbour.
Wills Memorial Building
A soaring neo-Gothic tower belonging to the University of Bristol, resembling a cathedral and one of the city's most photogenic silhouettes.
Christmas Steps
A charming, steep 17th-century cobbled lane lined with independent shops, one of Bristol's most picturesque historic streets.
Bristol Harbourside
The revitalized floating harbour area with colorful waterside buildings, the M Shed museum, and views of tall ships and cranes.
Banksy's Well Hung Lover
A famous piece of stencil street art by Bristol-born Banksy on Park Street, symbolizing the city's status as a global street art capital.

train.note: No international trains - Eurostar runs from London St Pancras only. GWR reaches London Paddington in about 1h20 from Bristol Temple Meads, with CrossCountry services north to Birmingham and beyond and local trains to Bath in 15 minutes. Bristol Parkway on the northern edge handles some Welsh and northbound services. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches; continental services connect via London. National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/) and FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.co.uk/) run from Bristol Bus & Coach Station to cities across Britain, with London in about 2h30 and Cardiff in an hour.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Bristol - Avonmouth and Royal Portbury are container and car-import docks. The Bristol Ferry Boats service on the Floating Harbour is a hop-on waterbus around the city centre rather than transport out of it. The nearest international crossings are from Poole and Portsmouth.

half.name: Bath
half.blurb: Georgian spa city with Roman-era bathhouses and honey-colored crescents, a short train ride from Bristol.

half.name: Cheddar Gorge
half.blurb: Limestone gorge and cave system in the Mendip Hills, home to England's deepest natural gorge and ancient caverns.

half.name: Stonehenge
half.blurb: Prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain, one of the world's most famous Neolithic monuments and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

half.name: Glastonbury
half.blurb: Market town linked to Arthurian legend, with the ruined abbey and Glastonbury Tor hill dominating the skyline.
